title: Planning an Okavango Delta Safari Around the Flood, the Camps and Your Budget
meta_title: Okavango Delta Safari Planner: Flood Months, Camps, Costs
meta_description: Plan an Okavango Delta safari: when the flood peaks, water vs land camps, Moremi vs private concessions, costs by tier and routes. Get a free quote.
excerpt: How to plan an Okavango Delta safari in Botswana: when the flood arrives, water camps versus land camps, Moremi versus private concessions, realistic costs and sample routes from Maun.
content:
An Okavango Delta safari is a trip into Botswana's great inland delta, explored by mokoro (dugout canoe), motorboat, on foot and in open vehicles. Most visitors fly in from Maun to a private camp for three to seven nights, and the best wildlife months run from June to October, when the flood is high and the bush is dry.

Planning one is harder than it looks. The Delta changes with the seasons, camps differ hugely in what they offer, and prices range from a few hundred dollars to several thousand per night. This guide explains how the flood works, water camps versus land camps, Moremi versus the private concessions, costs by tier and sample routes, so you can choose the right Okavango Delta safari for your dates and budget. For the wider country, see our Botswana safari guide for first-timers.

Quick Facts

  • Where: North-west Botswana; the gateway town is Maun
  • Size: The UNESCO World Heritage property covers about 20,000 km², with around 6,000 km² of permanent marsh
  • Peak flood: Around July; high water from roughly May to September
  • Best wildlife months: June to October (dry season)
  • Getting in: Light aircraft from Maun, about 15-45 minutes; or road to Moremi, about 3 hours
  • Luggage on light aircraft: 20 kg per person in a soft bag
  • Moremi entry fee: P270 per non-resident adult per day (checked November 2026)

What Makes an Okavango Delta Safari Different?

An Okavango Delta safari is different because water shapes everything. The Okavango River flows inland from Angola and spreads into a maze of channels, lagoons and islands in the Kalahari instead of reaching the sea, so you see wildlife from a canoe or on foot as well as from a vehicle.

The Delta became the 1,000th site on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014. UNESCO records 482 bird species there and describes the Delta as a core area for Botswana's elephants, alongside healthy numbers of lion, cheetah, wild dog and both rhino species. Seasonal grassland floods across up to 12,000 km² in a good year.

The other thing that sets an Okavango Delta safari apart is the way tourism is run. Most of the Delta is divided into large concessions leased to a handful of camps, and Botswana has long favoured fewer, higher-paying visitors. The result is very few vehicles at a sighting and a quiet that is hard to find in the busier parks of East Africa, but also some of the highest nightly rates on the continent.

When Is the Best Time for an Okavango Delta Safari?

The best time for an Okavango Delta safari is June to October, when floodwater fills the channels, the surrounding bush is dry and animals gather on the islands and floodplains. November to March is the green season: hotter and wetter, with lower water but lower prices, newborn animals and excellent birding.

How the flood shapes an Okavango Delta safari

The Okavango flood arrives in the dry season, which surprises most first-time visitors. Rain falls in the Angolan highlands from about November to March. The water then takes roughly four months to travel south, reaching Botswana's Panhandle between March and May, spreading through the Delta in the following weeks and usually peaking around July. Visible open water can grow from well under 1,000 km² in the driest months to over 7,000 km² at the peak.

The flood size changes from year to year with the Angolan rains, so camps on the edges of the Delta sometimes have a big flood and sometimes very little. If mokoro trips are the reason for your Okavango Delta safari, ask your planner about the current year's water before you book a seasonal camp.

Okavango Delta safari conditions by month

MonthsWater and weatherWhat it suits

April-MayRains end; floodwater reaching the Panhandle and spreadingShoulder-season value, lush scenery

Water Camps, Land Camps or Both?

Water camps sit in the permanent wetlands and focus on mokoro trips, motorboat excursions and island walks. Land camps sit on drier ground and focus on game drives. Mixed camps offer both. For a first Okavango Delta safari, splitting your nights between a water camp and a land camp gives the fullest picture.

A water camp is the classic Okavango Delta safari image: gliding through papyrus and water lilies with a poler standing at the back of the mokoro, reed frogs calling and an African fish eagle overhead. Big game sightings are less reliable here, and the pace is slow and quiet. It suits photographers, birders and anyone who has already done several vehicle safaris elsewhere.

On an Okavango Delta safari, a land camp is where most of the big cat and wild dog sightings come from. Game drives cover more ground, and in the private concessions guides can usually leave the road to follow a sighting and drive after dark. If you only have time for one camp and want predators, choose a land camp or a mixed camp that offers both drives and water activities in your month.

How a typical day runs

Days on an Okavango Delta safari follow a simple rhythm. You wake before sunrise for tea and a light breakfast, head out for the morning activity while it is cool, return for brunch and a rest in the heat, then go out again in the late afternoon. Many camps end the day with a sundowner on an island or the water before dinner.

Moremi Game Reserve or a Private Concession?

Moremi Game Reserve is the protected area in the east of the Delta, open to self-drivers, mobile safaris and lodges. The private concessions around it are leased to individual camps. For an Okavango Delta safari on a budget, Moremi is cheaper and easier to reach by road, while the concessions offer more privacy and freedom.

Moremi covers roughly 4,900 km² and is excellent for wildlife, especially around Xakanaxa, Third Bridge and the Khwai River. As a national reserve it has stricter rules: driving is on set tracks, there are no night drives and walking is not offered. Sightings at popular spots can attract several vehicles.

The private concessions work differently. Each one is shared by only a few camps, so vehicles are few and guides can drive off-road, run night drives and, where the land allows, lead walks. Khwai, next to Moremi's northern boundary, sits in between: a community area where night drives and off-road driving are allowed with qualified guides, often at lower prices than the big private concessions.

Off-road drivingNot allowedAllowed to follow sightings

If you are deciding between the Delta and Botswana's other big name, our comparison of the Okavango Delta and Chobe covers which suits your style. Many travellers end up doing both, finishing in Chobe or at Victoria Falls; our Chobe safari planning guide covers that leg.

How Much Does an Okavango Delta Safari Cost?

An Okavango Delta safari costs roughly US$600 to US$4,000 per person per night at fly-in camps, depending on the camp tier and season, with the highest rates in July and August. Mobile camping safaris in Moremi and short mokoro camping trips from Maun cost far less.

Most fly-in camps sell an Okavango Delta safari on fully inclusive rates covering meals, drinks, activities, park or concession fees and airstrip transfers. Seasonality makes a huge difference: the same camp can cost less than half as much in the green season as in peak months. The figures below are our estimates per person per night sharing, built from published camp rate bands for the current year; always ask for an exact quote.

StyleGreen season (estimate)Peak season (estimate)

Park fees and extras

For Moremi Game Reserve, the government entry fee for a non-resident adult is P270 per day, with children aged 8 to 15 at half price and under-8s free (checked November 2026). Campers pay a separate government camping fee plus the campsite operator's own charge, and campsites must be booked before you arrive at the gate.

Botswana planned large park and tourism fee rises for April 2026, but the government postponed them after objections from the tourism industry, and no new date had been set when we checked in November 2026. Fees could still change, so confirm the current rates before you book. Light aircraft seats from Maun to the camps add roughly US$220 to US$260 per person each way when they are not included in the camp rate.

How to Get There and How Many Days to Plan

Most Okavango Delta safari trips start in Maun, which has scheduled flights from Johannesburg and Cape Town. From Maun, small aircraft reach most camps in 15 to 45 minutes, and the road to Moremi's South Gate takes about three hours. Plan at least three nights, and ideally five to seven.

Airlink and Air Botswana fly to Maun from Johannesburg, and Airlink also flies from Cape Town. Travellers coming from Chobe can fly from Kasane, or road transfers can be arranged. Light aircraft transfers are shuttles that may stop at other airstrips on the way, so allow flexibility on timings.

Luggage is the detail most people get wrong on an Okavango Delta safari. Mack Air, which operates many Delta transfers, sets a limit of 20 kg per person including hand luggage, with soft bags preferred and a maximum size of 30 by 35 by 70 cm. Our safari packing checklist works well for Botswana too if you keep it to the lighter end.

Sample Okavango Delta safari routes

LengthRouteWho it suits
3 nightsMaun, then one water or mixed campA short add-on to Victoria Falls or Chobe
5-6 nightsMaun, water camp (2-3 nights), land camp in a concession or Khwai (3 nights)First-timers who want both mokoro and predators
8-10 nightsMaun, water camp, Moremi or Khwai, then Chobe and Victoria FallsA complete Botswana trip in one go

Insider Tips

  • Book early for July-September: Many Delta camps have only a handful of tents, and peak dates sell out a year or more ahead
  • Check the water activities: Ask each camp which activities run in your month; seasonal camps may not offer mokoro trips in low water
  • Mix your camps: A water camp plus a land camp beats two similar camps
  • Pack soft and light: Use a soft duffel bag of 20 kg or less, including your camera bag
  • Dress in layers: June and July mornings on an open vehicle or boat can be very cold
  • Consider the green season: January to March can bring big savings, lush scenery and good birding if you can accept some rain

Who Does the Delta Suit Best?

The Okavango suits travellers who value quiet, small camps and variety over ticking off animals fast. It is less suited to travellers on a tight budget who want guaranteed Big Five sightings in a few days. If you are weighing Botswana against Namibia, read our Etosha vs Okavango comparison.

Families should check camp age limits, as many water camps and walking activities have minimum ages. Mokoro trips are calm, but you sit low in the water and must keep still, so they suit patient children better than very young ones. Travellers with limited mobility should know that the small aircraft and some mokoro stations involve steps and getting into low boats.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need for an Okavango Delta safari?

An Okavango Delta safari needs at least three nights, because the first and last days are partly spent on transfers from Maun. Five to seven nights is better: you can split your stay between a water camp for mokoro and boating and a land camp for game drives, seeing both sides of the Delta.

Is the Okavango Delta worth the cost?

The Okavango Delta is expensive because Botswana keeps visitor numbers low, but most travellers find the quiet, the water activities and the quality of guiding worth it. If budget is tight, a mobile camping trip in Moremi or a short mokoro camping trip from Maun gives you the Delta for a fraction of private concession rates.

Can you do a mokoro trip all year in the Okavango Delta?

Mokoro trips run all year in the permanent channels of the Okavango Delta, but in seasonal areas they depend on the flood. Many camps on the edges of the Delta only offer mokoro excursions when the floodwater is in, roughly from May or June to September or October. Ask each camp what water activities it offers in your travel month.

When is the Okavango Delta flood at its highest?

The Okavango Delta flood is usually highest around July. Rain falls in the Angolan highlands from about November to March, and the water takes roughly four months to travel south, so it reaches the Panhandle between March and May and spreads across the Delta through the dry winter months, with high water from about May to September.

What is the luggage limit for flights into Okavango Delta camps?

Light aircraft flights into Okavango Delta camps usually allow 20 kg per person including hand luggage, packed in a soft bag without wheels or a rigid frame. Mack Air, which flies many Delta transfers, lists maximum bag dimensions of 30 cm by 35 cm by 70 cm. Pack light and leave extra luggage in Maun.

Final Thoughts

A good Okavango Delta safari is planned around the water. Go between June and October for high water and the best game, or in the green season for value, and mix a water camp with a land camp. Even a short mokoro camping trip from Maun shows you why this delta is unlike anywhere else in Africa.
